---
title: "Principles"
subtitle: "Where the efficiency gains come from, from one user's experience."
---

So I thought I will put my thoughts in here after our department meeting
with the help of Claude Code. Most of this is based on my experience of
using chatbot AI and agentic AI. So most of my thoughts are based on my
usage of LLM products from Anthropic (Claude, Claude Code), OpenAI (Chat
GPT, Codex) and a little of Github (Github copilot). I use Claude most of
the times. The efficiency gains that can be had depends heavily on how our
workflow is aligned with how large language models (LLMs) work.

The difference between chatbot AI tools like Claude (and Chat GPT) and
agentic AI like Claude code (and Codex) is that in the former you are in a
chat session and in the latter the AI does stuff on your behalf and uses
your computer to implement stuff using Bash scripts, after you give it
directory level permissions to run things. The major efficiency gains come
from using agentic AI over chatbot AI. In the latter there is a wide
variety of how much you let your LLM do your work. I used to think that
this depends on how risk averse you are. But in my experience, I think it
more depends on how detailed your prompting is such that the LLM
understands the context, how robust your system such that it has
fail-safes, and how do you design your workflow so that the agent can
verify its own work and can hence iterate on its mistakes minimizing your
intervention.

The rest of this page expands on those three things, because they are what
I would have wanted someone to tell me a year ago.

::: {.callout-note}
The pages on this site are organized around these three principles. The
[examples](examples/latex-paper.qmd) show what they look like in practice;
the [workflow](workflow/how-to-ask.qmd) and [pitfalls](pitfalls/hallucinations.qmd)
sections are the operational consequences. If you only have time for one
page besides this one, read the
[replication-package example](examples/replication-package.qmd) — it puts
all three principles to work at once.
:::

## 1. Detailed prompting and context

The single biggest predictor of whether Claude Code does something useful
on the first try is whether I gave it enough context to understand what I
actually want. "Detailed prompting" means giving the model the information
a smart RA would need to do the job — the relevant files, the constraints,
the goal. Length has nothing to do with it.

In practice, this is three things:

- **Name the files.** "Read `paper.tex` and tell me…" beats "look at my
  paper" every time. The model can find files; it cannot read your mind
  about which one you mean.
- **State the constraint, not just the goal.** "Reformat all my tables
  using booktabs" is the goal. "Reformat all my tables using booktabs;
  do not change any numbers, captions, or column headers" is the
  constraint that prevents Claude from "tidying up" content you didn't
  ask it to tidy.
- **Provide stable context once, not every session.** A `CLAUDE.md` file
  at the root of your project — saying which Stata version you use,
  which scripts produce which outputs, what's off-limits — is read at
  the start of every session. Writing it once saves you re-explaining.
  See [Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills](workflow/memory-and-claude-md.qmd).

The mental model that helped me: a chatbot prompt is a Google query, but
an agentic prompt is a memo to a new RA on day one. Different audience,
different register.

What this looks like in our examples:

- The first paragraph of every prompt in the [LaTeX paper
  walkthrough](examples/latex-paper.qmd) is an orientation pass — having
  Claude read the project before doing anything.
- The [replication-package audit](examples/replication-package.qmd) starts
  by asking Claude to *describe* the dependency map before *changing*
  anything. The audit is the context for the action.

## 2. A robust system with fail-safes

This was the principle that took me longest to internalize because it
requires admitting up front that the model will sometimes do the wrong
thing — and designing your environment so a wrong action is recoverable
rather than catastrophic.

The fail-safes I rely on are not exotic:

- **Git, even just locally.** I commit before any non-trivial change. If
  Claude makes an edit I don't like, `git checkout .` undoes everything
  in the working directory. You don't need to push to GitHub for this to
  save you. (New to Git? The [Git page](getting-started/git.qmd) is the
  shortest path from zero to using it as a daily safety net.)
- **Plan mode.** For any change touching multiple files, I hit
  `Shift+Tab` until the prompt says "plan mode". Claude reads, thinks,
  and writes a plan for my approval. I read the plan; if it misunderstands,
  I correct before any file is touched. See [Plan mode, todos, slash
  commands](getting-started/plan-mode-and-todo.qmd).
- **Don't blanket-allow destructive operations.** Claude Code prompts
  before things like deleting files, force-pushing to git, or running
  `rm -rf`. Don't override those prompts. The two-second pause is the
  difference between a recoverable mistake and a Saturday spent
  reconstructing your project from memory.
- **A working "master script" in every project.** A single `master.do`,
  `master.R`, or `make all` that rebuilds your results from scratch.
  After any meaningful change, ask Claude to re-run it and confirm
  outputs match. This is your reproducibility check *and* your fail-safe.
- **Read-only patterns for restricted data.** When I work on projects
  with IRB-protected or restricted-access data, Claude only ever sees the
  *code*, never the data. The data lives in a folder Claude is not
  pointed at. See [Confidential data](pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd).

A useful test: before starting a task, ask yourself "if Claude does the
worst plausible thing here, what is my recovery?" If the answer is "git
checkout", you're fine. If the answer is "rebuild from backups" or "email
my coauthor", slow down and add a fail-safe first.

## 3. A workflow the agent can verify on its own

This is the principle with the highest payoff and the one most colleagues
miss: **structure the task so the agent can check its own work**, and it
can iterate on its mistakes without needing you in the loop for every step.

A few examples of what this looks like in econ work:

- **Replication.** "Re-run `master.do` and tell me whether each table in
  `output/tables/` matches the version checked into git." The agent runs
  the script, diffs the outputs, and either reports "all match" or "Table
  3 changed — here's the diff". One human-readable status; no per-step
  babysitting.
- **Cleaning.** Add assertions to your cleaning scripts:
  `assert wage > 0 if inrange(year, 2000, 2020)`. When Claude edits the
  cleaning code and an assertion fails, the script halts and the agent
  sees exactly what broke. It can iterate to fix the bug without you.
- **LaTeX.** After every edit to a `.tex` file, Claude can compile and
  read the log. Unresolved references, overfull boxes, missing citations
  — all surface immediately, and the agent can either fix them or escalate
  to you.
- **Numerical work.** A test that checks the sign and rough magnitude of
  the main coefficient (not its exact value) is enough for Claude to
  notice when a refactor silently breaks the analysis.
- **Code review.** For non-trivial edits I ask Claude to run `/review`
  on its own diff before showing it to me. It catches its own clumsy
  edits about half the time.

When this principle is in place, my supervision shifts from "every
keystroke" to "every milestone". I check in when the agent reports
something done, not while it works.

## Putting it together

These three principles compound. Detailed prompting is wasted if the
agent can't recover from a wrong turn. Fail-safes keep you safe but not
productive. Self-verification is impossible without context to verify
against. Roughly:

> efficiency ≈ (quality of context) × (recoverability of the system) ×
> (degree to which the agent can check its own work)

If any factor is near zero, the product is too — the model being capable
doesn't help. Most of my own learning has been about raising the third
factor: the model is capable enough; the bottleneck was giving it the
scaffolding to work without me hovering over it.
